version.changelog: Initial release: OAuth2 auth, task/project CRUD, batch operations, rate limit handling

vt.analysis:
Type: OpenClaw Skill
Name: ticktick
Version: 1.0.0

The OpenClaw AgentSkills skill bundle for TickTick is benign. It provides a command-line interface for managing TickTick tasks and projects, utilizing standard OAuth2 for authentication. Credentials (client ID/secret, access/refresh tokens) are stored in the designated secure location `~/.clawdbot/credentials/ticktick-cli/config.json` with restrictive file permissions (0o600). All network communication is directed to the legitimate TickTick API (`https://api.ticktick.com/open/v1` and `https://ticktick.com/oauth`). The `SKILL.md` documentation provides clear, non-malicious instructions for both human users and AI agents, with no evidence of prompt injection attempts or instructions to perform unauthorized actions. There is no indication of data exfiltration, malicious execution, persistence, or obfuscation.

llm.summary: This is a coherent TickTick command-line skill, but it handles TickTick OAuth secrets and can change tasks, so users should treat its local config and mutation commands carefully.

dimensions.detail: Outbound TickTick API calls, a localhost OAuth callback server, browser opening, and a home-directory credential file are proportionate to the OAuth CLI purpose, but they require user awareness.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The package metadata shows a Bun CLI with commander and open dependencies, no install hook, and no hidden setup behavior beyond user-invoked scripts.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The instructions disclose API use, token storage, and mutating commands; however, abandon and batch-abandon are presented as normal commands without a prominent confirmation or dry-run warning.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: The skill persists OAuth client credentials and access/refresh tokens in plaintext JSON with attempted 0700/0600 permissions, discloses this in SKILL.md, and logout clears tokens while preserving client credentials.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

dimensions.detail: The stated purpose is TickTick task and project management, and the inspected code implements OAuth authentication plus task/project listing, creation, update, completion, and abandon operations against the TickTick API.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

llm.guidance: Install only if you are comfortable granting TickTick task read/write access. Avoid pasting real client secrets into shared terminals or automation logs, protect ~/.clawdbot/credentials/ticktick-cli/config.json, and verify task IDs carefully before using abandon or batch-abandon.
llm.findings:
[LP3] expected: Shell-invoked CLI use and network access are expected for this command-line TickTick integration, and the artifact discloses TickTick API usage; no hidden remote payload or privilege expansion was found.
[SQP-2] expected: Abandon and batch-abandon are purpose-aligned task-management operations, but users should verify task IDs because the commands modify remote task state without an added confirmation step.
[RA2] expected: Persistent OAuth session storage is expected for a reusable CLI and is disclosed, but plaintext refresh-token and client-secret storage remains a real local credential-handling risk.
[T09] unexpected: Accepting the OAuth client secret directly as a command-line argument is an avoidable exposure path through shell history or process logs, though it is not evidence of deception or exfiltration.
[T09] expected: Plaintext credential and token storage is disclosed and permission-restricted, but users should treat the config file as sensitive and avoid syncing or backing it up insecurely.
[T09] unexpected: The manual OAuth error path can print the pasted redirect URL on failure, which may expose a short-lived authorization code in logs; this is a handling weakness rather than malicious behavior.
